To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) The prevalence of depression among elderly patients is high; (ii) Depression is underdiagnosed in the elderly; (iii) The elderly are at increased risk for depression because of the high prevalence of medical illnesses, disability, and functional impairments in this age group; (iv) Depression is often associated with other medical illnesses, and it can be difficult to differentiate depression from the effects of medical illness on mood; (v) Depression is often misdiagnosed as dementia;
the use of the term “geriatric” is associated with a negative connotation and that the term “gerontology” is associated with more favorable connotations.

the elderly patients in our study had a higher prevalence of psychiatric illness than did younger adults, that they had more severe psychiatric symptoms and a higher level of impairment, and that they were more likely to have multiple physical disorders.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the elderly patient is not a problem, but rather a person who presents problems, many of which are not unique to the elderly, but are simply more frequent and more severe.
geriatric psychiatry is a specialty in which a general psychiatist can become expert and in which a specialist can become an authority.
the geriatric patient presents a unique challenge to the general hospital psychiatrist.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the general hospital psychiatry is an important part of the health care system and has an important role in the care of geriatric patients.

geriatric patients present special problems for the general hospital psychiatrist because of their high incidence on medical and surgical units, the special problems they present in the psychiatric setting, the special problems in the use of medication, and the special problems in dealing with their families and caregivers.

geriatric patients are more likely to be on medical and surgical units, more likely to have multiple physical and mental disorders, more likely to be treated by nonpsychiatric staff, and more likely to require special treatment and care than younger patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the geriatric population is large and growing, and general hospital psychiatrists need be especially knowledgeable about issues presented by these patients because of their large proportion on medical and psychiatric services.
geriatric patients are more likely to have a higher number of chronic diseases and more severe functional limitations than younger adults.
there is a great need for a better understanding of how to treat older patients on general hospital psychiatric units.
